summary:
Armenia carries no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct; the provision was repealed in 2003, and the country has no statute of the restrictive type applied to LGBT people in neighbouring Azerbaijan. Trans visitors face no legal exposure for being trans, but the legal framework offers them little affirmative protection: there is no discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the anti-discrimination bill tabled in 2018 did not pass.

Legal gender recognition exists as an administrative practice and is medicalised. Equaldex records that a legal gender change has been available since 2006 but requires surgery, that gender-affirming care is restricted, and that no non-binary recognition is available. Hate-crime protection covering bias-motivated violence is characterised as ambiguous since 2022, and same-sex marriage is prohibited.

Pink Human Rights Defender NGO's annual report on the human rights situation of LGBT+ people in Armenia during 2024 documents discrimination, torture and inhuman or degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion, violations of private and family life, and discrimination in education and work. It records hate speech as a persistent feature of public discourse and devotes a chapter to the pressure directed at a transgender individual who participated in a beauty pageant.

Trans people in positions of visibility have drawn extreme political hostility. In April 2019 Lilit Martirosyan, Armenia's first registered trans woman, received death threats after delivering a speech on LGBTI discrimination in the national assembly; members of parliament called for her to be burned alive.

Enforcement of violence against LGBT spaces is unreliable. In May 2012 a Molotov cocktail was thrown at the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan and a fire set; police took twelve hours to respond, though two suspects were later detained through CCTV footage. Equaldex's public-opinion measure puts acceptance at 5 out of 100, indicating a social environment where visible trans presence draws hostility well beyond central Yerevan.

The capital has an organised community, with Pink Armenia and the trans-led organisation Right Side operating locally. Visibility outside those networks remains a source of risk rather than protection.
tangentialFactors:
Regional comparison matters for expectation-setting: Equaldex's three-way comparison of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia places Armenia at the decriminalised end of the spectrum, while Azerbaijan retains criminalisation. A visitor crossing the border should not read Armenia's domestic tolerance as a regional norm.

The institutional picture has been documented for a long period. The ILGA-Europe and COC fact-finding mission report 'Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia' (February 2009) covers societal and institutional homophobia, media coverage, discrimination, harassment and violence, and the state of legislation affecting LGBT people; the 2024 findings above indicate that several of those patterns persist fifteen years on.

Public hostility is not confined to informal settings. The 2019 threats against Lilit Martirosyan originated from serving members of parliament, and the 2024 report records organised pressure around a trans person's participation in a public event.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking legal gender recognition must complete a medicalised administrative procedure, and the change is conditioned on surgery. Gender-affirming care is restricted in availability, and there is no legal category for non-binary people.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, education, housing or services, since the 2018 anti-discrimination bill failed. Hate-crime treatment of bias-motivated attacks is ambiguous, which affects the recourse available after violence.

LGBT residents documented in Pink Armenia's 2024 report continue to face inhuman or degrading treatment, including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion, alongside violations of private and family life. Pink Armenia and Right Side provide the principal organised support and advocacy in Yerevan.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses Armenian border control, visa issuance or document-screening practice as it affects trans travellers, including what happens if a passport gender marker does not match presentation. That question remains unresolved here.

The requirement that legal gender change be preceded by surgery is sourced to Equaldex, a comparison aggregator, rather than to the text of the Armenian legislation itself; the governing statute was not supplied for verification. The same applies to the characterisation of hate-crime protection as 'ambiguous since 2022' and to the restricted status of gender-affirming care.

The 5/100 public-acceptance figure comes from Equaldex's methodology and has not been corroborated against an Armenian polling source. The ILGA-Europe/COC mission report dates from 2009 and describes conditions at that time rather than the present.
